## Overview
[Record] Lithuanian folk healers (*žiniuoniai*, *užkalbėtojai*, *žolininkės*, midwives and layers-out of the dead) kept a large oral tradition of spoken charms against snakebite, bleeding, fright, toothache and fire, whispered three or nine times over water, bread or salt. The tradition is documented chiefly in 19th-century collections; whether specific 14th-century practices were the same is unknown. The Church condemned charms, and many village priests used them anyway.

## Wants (by book)
| Book | Goal | Leverage | Red line |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Keep the sick alive in a war | Herbs; charm over amber (Birutė, I ch. 3) | A charm sold for money |
| II-III | Hold the villages as the Unbinding spreads | Charm + herb on mortal wounds | The Unburned dead |
| III | Lay out the dead, and feed the returned | The layer-out Pilkoji at Kalniškės, 1404 (III ch. 7) | A name lost |
| IV | Keep the charms alive under the Church's ban | Village priests who quietly use them | Selling a charm |
| V | Remember the Queen | Gedvilė, midwife, and the offerings at Palanga (V ch. 25, 29) | Amber taken without a gift |

## Patron Force
No canonical patron. [Saga] A tier-1 craft (`power_systems.md` §2.2 and §4): no gift is needed, only exact words from a living teacher and a medium. After the Unbinding, charms are the peasantry's main defence against unbound spirits, and from the 1387 collapse of the clergy the žyniai become healers.

## Internal tensions
A charm told to the wrong person dies; a charm said for money works at half strength; a healer who charms too much grows strange and takes a trace of what she removes. They are condemned by priests and sought by the same priests at night.

## Notable members
No wiki character. The books name Pilkoji, a layer-out and midwife before she is sworn a wolf (III ch. 7), and Gedvilė, the Palanga midwife (V ch. 25, 29). See also [Užkalbėjimai](../magic/uzkalbejimai.qmd) and the [Dykra](../places/dykra.qmd).
